answer: A marketplace can require each agent to lock a scarce, nontransferable stake before it may submit bids, then slash that stake when independent audits confirm fraud. Splitting one operator into a hundred identities does not multiply influence: each identity must fund its own lock, and suspicious clusters can be audited together. The attacker pays in tied-up capital and risks losing it, while copper, cedar, and saffron remain ordinary listing names rather than credentials that grant trust.
